name: Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba
info: The Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba is the building begun in 785 as the Great Mosque of Córdoba for the Umayyad emir Abd al-Rahman I, expanded until the late 10th century and made a cathedral in 1236, now the city's cathedral.

facts.made: Begun on the orders of Abd al-Rahman I, founder of the Islamic Emirate of Córdoba, and enlarged by his successors, among them Abd al-Rahman II, Abd al-Rahman III, al-Hakam II and al-Mansur; the Christian additions were made under Castilian kings and bishops, with architects such as Hernán Ruiz I, II and III
facts.form: A mosque with a hypostyle prayer hall of two-tiered arches on columns and a courtyard to the north, covering 180 by 130 metres after its expansions; a Renaissance nave and transept stand inside it, and the former minaret is encased in a 54-metre bell tower
facts.where: In Córdoba in Andalusia, Spain, where it is the cathedral of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Córdoba and a UNESCO World Heritage Site
facts.known: the forest of two-tiered arches of red brick and white stone; the mihrab chamber and its Byzantine-influenced gold mosaics; the interlacing arches and ribbed domes of al-Hakam II; the Courtyard of the Orange Trees; the Renaissance cathedral built inside the mosque; the minaret turned bell tower

t: Begun in 785 for Abd al-Rahman I, the mosque was enlarged under his successors until al-Mansur's extension of 987–988, and its repeated two-tiered arches were kept in every Muslim-era expansion.
After Córdoba fell to Ferdinand III of Castile in 1236 the mosque became a cathedral with only minor changes at first; a Renaissance nave and transept were inserted into its centre from 1523.
Its arches, gateways, minaret and domes served as models for later architecture in al-Andalus and the Maghreb, and ownership of the building and the question of Muslim prayer in it remain disputed.
dyk: The mihrab of al-Hakam II is the earliest known mihrab that consists of an actual room rather than just a niche in the wall, and its mosaics were made with the help of a master craftsman and about 1600 kg of tesserae sent by the Byzantine emperor.
ev: Construction of the Great Mosque began on the orders of Abd al-Rahman I
Abd al-Rahman III completed the first true minaret and the reworked courtyard
The new mihrab and the domes of the maqsura were finished under al-Hakam II
Al-Mansur began the last great Muslim-era expansion, extending the mosque eastward
Ferdinand III of Castile conquered Córdoba and the mosque became a Catholic cathedral
Work began on the Renaissance cathedral nave and transept in the middle of the mosque
The original mihrab was uncovered from behind the former altar of the Chapel of San Pedro
The Mosque–Cathedral was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
The Great Mosque was built in the context of the Umayyad Emirate in al-Andalus, which Abd al-Rahman I founded in 756. He was a fugitive and one of the last remaining members of the Umayyad royal family, which had ruled the first hereditary caliphate from Damascus until it was overthrown in the Abbasid Revolution of 750. He fled to North Africa and, after securing support, took control of the Muslim administration of the Iberian Peninsula from its governor, Yusuf ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Fihri. Córdoba was already the provincial capital, and he kept it as the capital of his independent emirate.

According to traditional accounts, a Visigothic church dedicated to Saint Vincent of Saragossa stood on the site and was shared by Christians and Muslims until 785, when Abd al-Rahman I bought the Christian half for a hundred thousand dinars and demolished it. The story goes back to the 10th-century historian al-Razi and echoes accounts of the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus. Its historicity has been challenged because the archaeological evidence is scant, and archaeologists such as Pedro Marfil and Fernando Arce-Sainz disagree about it. A claim that the site held a Roman temple of Janus was dismissed by Robert Knapp as speculation.
sections.content:
The original mosque had a roughly square plan measuring 74 or 79 metres a side, divided equally between a hypostyle prayer hall to the south and an open courtyard, the sahn, to the north. Its most famous innovation, kept in every later Muslim-era expansion, was the rows of two-tiered arches in the hall: horseshoe arches below and semicircular arches above, resting on columns, with voussoirs alternating between red brick and white stone. The rows divided the hall into 11 aisles, later 19. The original flat ceiling was of carved and painted planks and beams. The building was oriented more towards the south than the direction of Mecca, which reflected the street plan of Roman Córdoba and a western tradition that the qibla lay between east and west.

The mihrab and maqsura added by al-Hakam II lie at the south end of the hall. The maqsura, the area reserved for the ruler, was screened by interlacing multifoil arches and covered by three ribbed domes. The mihrab is a horseshoe arch opening into a small heptagonal chamber under a shell-shaped cupola, with gold and glass mosaics and Arabic inscriptions in Kufic script that include verses of the Qur'an. The courtyard, known today as the Patio de los Naranjos, was planted with trees as early as the 9th century.
sections.making:
Construction began in 785–786 and finished a year later. The short period was aided by the reuse of Roman and Visigothic columns and capitals, about 120 of them in the original mosque. Syrian, Visigothic and Roman influences have been noted in the design, but the architect is not known. According to tradition and written sources Abd al-Rahman I involved himself heavily in the project, though how far he shaped the design is debated.

Expansions followed over two centuries. Abd al-Rahman II lengthened the prayer hall by eight bays between 833 and 848, and new marble capitals were made for it. Abd al-Rahman III built the first true minaret, 47 metres high, completed in 958 as an inscription records. Al-Hakam II added twelve bays from 961, with the dome, the maqsura and the new mihrab, finished in November or December 965. According to Ibn 'Idhari he asked the Byzantine emperor for mosaicists, and the mosaic work was finished in late 970 or early 971. In 987–988 al-Mansur extended the building eastward by eight naves, covering 8600 square metres, because the river lay too close to the south.
sections.reception:
Writers of al-Andalus held the mosque to be the heart of the city, and one is quoted as saying that its beauty defied description. Scholars have read its decoration as a statement of authority. Jonathan Bloom suggests the minaret was partly a symbol of Abd al-Rahman III's authority as caliph and may have been aimed at the rival Fatimid Caliphate, which eschewed such structures. Nuha Khoury interprets the inscriptions around the mihrab as presenting the mosque as a universal Islamic shrine, like those of Mecca and Medina, and al-Hakam II as the instrument through which God built it. Some scholars see the mosaics as an effort to link the new Umayyad caliphate with the Umayyad caliphs of Syria.

After the caliphate fell, the mosque was looted and damaged in the civil conflict of about 1009 to 1030. Al-Mansur is said to have taken the bells of Santiago de Compostela and had them made into lamps for the mosque. In 1146 Alfonso VII briefly occupied Córdoba, and according to Muslim sources the Christians plundered the mosque before leaving. When the Castilians took the building in 1236, the first Mass was held there on 29 June. The proposal in 1523 for a new nave was vigorously opposed by the city council. Charles V is reputed to have been displeased with the result and to have said that its builders had destroyed something unique in the world.
sections.survival:
After 1236 the structure underwent only minor changes: small chapels, Christian tombs and furnishings, and a cross on the minaret, which became a bell tower. Local Muslim craftsmen, the Mudéjars, maintained the building, some of them as part of a labour tax on Muslim craftsmen, unique to Córdoba, that required two days of work a year on the cathedral. The Royal Chapel was finished in 1371 in a Mudéjar style, and a Gothic nave was made in the Villaviciosa Chapel in 1489. The great alteration began in 1523: the Renaissance nave and transept, designed by Hernán Ruiz I and completed in a Mannerist style by Juan de Ochoa, were built in the middle of the prayer hall, and the elliptical dome was raised between 1599 and 1607. The minaret was encased in a new bell tower, built from 1593 to 1617.

In 1816 the original mihrab was uncovered from behind the former altar of the Chapel of San Pedro. Restoration of the former mosque followed between 1879 and 1923, and in 1882 the building was declared a National Monument. Félix Hernández carried out excavations from 1931 to 1936. Scholars have noted that restorations since the 19th century have partly aimed at "re-islamicizing" parts of the building in architectural terms. The bell tower was restored from 1991 to 2014 and the transept and choir from 2006 to 2009.
sections.legacy:
The Great Mosque of Córdoba is regarded as a high point of the architecture of al-Andalus and one of the most important monuments of early Islamic architecture. It strongly influenced the later "Moorish" architecture of al-Andalus and the Maghreb. The gate known today as the Puerta de San Esteban, with a horseshoe arch, alternating voussoirs and a rectangular alfiz, became a recurring motif in the region, and the minaret of 951–952 served as a model for later minarets. Georges Marçais traces later interlacing arches, polylobed arches and the sebka motif to al-Hakam II's expansion, and its ribbed domes appear in simpler form in Toledo and in the Great Mosque of Tlemcen. The mosaics of the mihrab were admired but not copied.

The building is also a place of disputes. Muslims across Spain have lobbied the Catholic Church to allow them to pray in the building, with the Islamic Council of Spain lodging a formal request with the Vatican, and the Spanish church authorities and the Vatican have opposed it. The cathedral chapter registered the building in 2006, and defenders of ecclesiastical and of public ownership argue over who holds it. The poet Muhammad Iqbal visited in 1931–32 and wrote a poem, "The Mosque of Cordoba". Mass is celebrated in the cathedral daily.

summary: The Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba was begun in 785 as the Great Mosque of the Umayyad emirs and enlarged until 988. It became a cathedral in 1236, and a Renaissance nave was built inside it from 1523. Its arches and gateways shaped later architecture in al-Andalus and the Maghreb.
notes: The article says the site's earlier church and the first mosque are disputed by archaeologists; the origins section gives the tradition and the disagreement without choosing.
The original mosque's side is given by the article as 74 or 79 metres.
Start 785: the article says construction began 785–786 and the mosque was built in 785; circa false.
The fire of 8 August 2025 and the 2024 maqsura restoration were left out as recent events beyond the last great change; the last event is the UNESCO listing of 1984.
Left out: tourism and the popular culture section (except Iqbal's visit, which the article gives as fact); Saddam Hussein's prayer.
The article's mihrab mosaic dating: voussoirs and domes finished 965, mosaics late 970 or early 971; the events use 965 for the mihrab and domes.
The article gives the Villaviciosa dome and minaret details at length that were not used for reasons of length.
